e.t: Abarim, also called Avarim, is a proper name preserved as a name rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Numbers 33. The name is associated with the place or named setting identified in those passages, though the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific role there. Its consistent rendering as “Abarim” confirms that the central meaning is the name itself.

This adjective means “rustic,” describing a person or thing as having a rustic character or manner. It functions as a descriptive word, so its precise force depends on what it modifies in the sentence. The Greek LXX uses this word three times: twice in Genesis and once in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains a straightforward description of something rustic, while the surrounding context determines whether the description is favorable, unfavorable, or simply factual.

Azmoth is a biblical proper name, identifying a person rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. The name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 23:31 and 1 Chronicles 11:33. The available lexical information gives the name as “Azmōth” or “Azmoth,” but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning. Its precise role in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This word means a point or barb—the sharp end or projecting part of something. It is a noun describing a pointed object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 16:10, so its wider range of use cannot be established from repeated appearances. The surrounding verse provides the context for understanding exactly what pointed object is meant there.

This adverb means “unreasonably,” describing speech or action that does not follow sound judgment or a sensible basis. It tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 3 Maccabees 6:25. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise force in that sentence cannot be expanded safely, but its central idea is conduct or reasoning that is irrational, unjustified, or contrary to good sense.

This proper noun refers to the people called “Amorraios” or “Amorreos,” the Amorites. It functions as a people-group name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 90 times across 86 verses, from Genesis through Amos. The name appears especially often in Joshua, Deuteronomy, Numbers, Judges, and Exodus, reflecting the repeated identification of this people in Israel’s historical account. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes someone who is shameless—acting without the restraint or embarrassment that normally comes from recognizing what is wrong or dishonorable. It can characterize a person whose conduct is openly bold in a bad sense, rather than quietly restrained. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twelve times, including passages from Deuteronomy, Proverbs, Isaiah, and other books. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a lack of shame or moral reserve.

This verb means “sprout up”: it describes something emerging and beginning to grow. It is a word of growth, used for what rises or appears from the ground or another source. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across six verses, so its basic sense remains focused and consistent rather than broad or abstract. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is sprouting, but the word itself emphasizes the act of coming up and developing.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut off,” describing the act of removing or severing something. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Hosea 6:5. The word’s basic sense is an action that brings something to an end by cutting it away. The precise force of the word in Hosea depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its lexical meaning remains straightforward: to cut off. It is not a general noun for separation, but a verb expressing the act itself.

Redemption refers to release or recovery from a condition of loss, bondage, or need. As a noun, it names the act or result of being redeemed. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, at Daniel 4:34, so its broader scriptural range cannot be established from repeated usage within this corpus. Its central idea remains redemption: an act of bringing someone or something out of an adverse condition and into a restored state. The precise force at Daniel 4:34 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek word means “mission,” naming a specific undertaking or assignment. It is a noun, so it identifies the mission itself rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament collection represented here, it appears nine times across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its central meaning remains consistent: a mission is something given or undertaken for a particular purpose. The precise force in any verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context.

gl: subject to a levy in money
d: subject to a levy in money

e.t: This Greek LXX noun refers to something subject to a levy in money—a payment assessed in currency. It describes a financial obligation rather than a person, action, or general quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 11:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: something designated for payment through a monetary levy.

This word is the proper name “Arphath,” also represented as “Arfath.” It functions as a name rather than a common description or action word, so its meaning is primarily identification: it names what is being referred to in the Greek Old Testament text. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in Isaiah—at Isaiah 36:19 and Isaiah 37:13. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify the named subject’s precise role there.

This Greek LXX verb means “high priest”: it describes serving or functioning in the role of the high priest. As a verb, it focuses on carrying out that office rather than simply naming the person who holds it. In this corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 14:47. The precise force of the word in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse text, but its central meaning is acting in the high-priestly role.

Assur is a proper name, rendered “Assur” or “Assour” in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. The name occurs 38 times across 36 verses in the Greek Old Testament, from Genesis through Micah. Its precise referent in any particular verse must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context; the name itself does not provide a broader abstract meaning.

This LXX adjective describes someone or something as “not disturbed” or “quiet.” It points to a state free from agitation, disruption, or unrest, and can describe settled circumstances or a calm condition. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, with two occurrences in Esther and one in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX adjective means “unwounded”: not injured or bearing a wound. It describes someone or something that has come through danger without physical harm. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX material represented here, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines whether it describes a person, group, or object as unharmed.

Achōchi, also rendered Akhokhi, is a proper name referring to a person. It is not a general term describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 11:12. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be described further. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the personal name itself, rather than as a word with a broader ordinary definition.

This adjective describes a voice as “of deep voice,” identifying a deep quality in the sound. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 33:19. Since the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding sentence, while its basic lexical sense remains connected with a deep voice.

Barachias, also rendered Varakhias, is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 11 times across 11 verses in the LXX, including genealogical, priestly, and prophetic settings, but the name itself does not state which individual is intended. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding passage and the person named there.

This noun means “that which is borne; burden”—something carried or borne by a person. It can refer to a physical load, but the basic word itself simply identifies what is being carried, without specifying whether the burden is heavy, difficult, or symbolic. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses, all within the Old Testament corpus. Its recognized English rendering is “burden.” The surrounding verse is needed to determine whether the word points to an object being transported or to a matter treated as a burden.

Bēthmaallōn, also rendered Vithmaallon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs twice in Judges 9:20, within the same verse. The available lexical information preserves the name but does not explain its location or significance, so its meaning is chiefly the identification of the named entity in that passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a person’s “livelihood” or “lifestyle”—the practical way someone lives and sustains daily life. It is used for life viewed in terms of one’s living circumstances, resources, or manner of life, rather than as a particular event or action. The word occurs 68 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this LXX corpus. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “calf,” referring to a young bovine animal. It is a noun, so it names the animal rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 27:11. The word’s basic meaning is clear, while the exact significance of the animal in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its translation context. By itself, the word identifies the animal without specifying its symbolic or practical role.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Gasiōngaber” or “Gasiongaver.” It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, and 2 Chronicles. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

This word is a proper name rendered “Gōim” or “Yim.” It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 12:23. The available information establishes its name forms but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain which person, group, or place it identifies there. Its precise reference therefore depends on reading Joshua 12:23 in context.

This Greek LXX noun means “skin.” It refers to the outer covering of a person or animal and can be spoken of as a single covering or as multiple skins. The word occurs 78 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, with especially frequent use in Leviticus, where skin is mentioned in connection with bodily examination and animal skins. Its basic meaning remains the physical skin or hide itself; the surrounding verse determines the specific object being discussed.

This Greek LXX noun means “message” or “notice”—information communicated so that others become aware of something. It names a communication rather than an action, person, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 5:1, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains a conveyed announcement or report intended to reach someone. Its lexical identity and meaning are recorded in the source-word data, with the occurrence reference confirming its single location.

This verb means “clear completely”: it describes making something fully clear rather than partially clarifying it. As a Greek Old Testament word, it occurs once in the Septuagint, at Nehemiah 8:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on surrounding wording, but its central idea remains complete clarification. It functions as an action word, expressing what someone does to another.

This noun refers to something “ash-baked”—food prepared by baking it in or among ashes. It describes a cooking method rather than an attitude, action, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs eight times, in eight verses. Its precise reference may depend on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains food or an item made by baking with ashes.

This noun means “eulogy,” referring to words of praise or commendation spoken or written in honor of someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Esther 2:23. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s exact role in that passage cannot be described further; its central meaning remains an expression of honor or praise. It is a distinct Greek LXX word, not a Greek New Testament entry.

This adjective describes someone or something that has been banished or cast away—removed from a place, community, or position. It presents exclusion as the defining condition, rather than merely describing distance or absence. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Jeremiah 22:30. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning is clear: a person or thing rejected and sent away.

This verb means “put out.” It describes an action in which something is caused to go out or is placed outside. Its precise force depends on what is being put out and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains an outward removal or placement. Within this LXX corpus, it occurs seven times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing a repeated but relatively uncommon action word.

Engaddi, also rendered Engaththi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 2 Chronicles 20:2. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise local significance cannot be explained here; its lexical meaning is the name itself.

This verb means “catching a snare,” expressing an action involving a snare. It is an action word, rather than the name of a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, at Job 40:24. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, its precise role in that sentence cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is “catching a snare.”

This verb means “verify”: to examine something so that its truth or accuracy can be established. It describes an act of checking rather than merely accepting a claim. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs 12 times, appearing in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Its use includes settings where statements, actions, or claims require careful confirmation. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being verified, but the central idea remains testing or examining something to establish whether it is reliable.

This verb means “arm completely; accoutre.” It describes the action of fully equipping someone for a task, especially by providing the necessary arms or equipment. The word appears twice in the LXX corpus, once in Numbers and once in 2 Maccabees, showing its use across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical Greek Scripture. As a verb, it expresses an action performed on someone or something rather than naming the equipment itself.

This verb means “challenge,” describing an act of confronting or rising against someone or something. It presents opposition as an action rather than merely naming a hostile attitude. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 35 times across 35 verses, showing that it is used in a range of passages where opposition or confrontation is expressed. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This noun means “throwing”: the act or movement of casting something from one place toward another. It names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 8:7. The basic meaning identifies the action, while the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “fly to”: it describes moving swiftly through the air toward a person or place. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Epistle of Jeremiah 1:21. The word’s basic sense is clear, while the exact force of that action in the verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “pack”: to gather or arrange things so they are ready to be carried or used. It is a practical action word, describing preparation rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. It occurs eight times in the LXX corpus represented here, including passages from Exodus, Samuel, Chronicles, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being prepared and the surrounding sentence.

This word means “worker”: a person who performs labor or carries out work. It is a noun, so it identifies the person doing the work rather than the work itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, it occurs 12 times, showing that it is a normal term for someone engaged in work. Its precise reference in any verse comes from the surrounding passage.

Eremmon is a proper name, preserved in English as “Eremmon.” It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word such as a verb, adjective, or common noun. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:7. The available information identifies the name and its occurrence, but does not provide the verse text or enough surrounding context to explain more about what Eremmon designates in that passage.

This adjective describes something occurring toward evening, as daylight is moving toward night. It gives a time reference rather than naming an action, person, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, all in seven different verses, and is rendered with the idea of evening in several of those passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary meaning remains a period approaching evening. It appears from Leviticus through Daniel, showing use across different kinds of Old Testament passages.

This Greek LXX noun means “benefit”: something helpful or favorable that a person receives or provides. It names the beneficial result itself rather than describing an action. The word appears six times in the supplied Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Psalms, Wisdom, and Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a benefit.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “grow luxuriantly”—to flourish with abundant, vigorous growth. It describes something that develops richly and impressively rather than merely existing or increasing a little. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Hosea 10:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is thriving, flourishing growth.

This Greek LXX adjective means “stout” or “strong,” describing someone or something possessing physical strength and solid vigor. It is a descriptive word rather than an action or command. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 30:15. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains the condition of being robust, sturdy, or strong.

“Sit in the court” is the meaning of this verb: it describes taking a seated place in a court. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs only once, in 2 Samuel 21:14. The phrase gives the word a specific everyday sense of sitting in a formal court setting, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular situation. This Greek LXX word should not be merged with similarly rendered Hebrew or Greek New Testament words.

Thamnatha is a proper name for a place. It is not presented here as a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but as the name of a location appearing in the Greek Old Testament and once in 1 Maccabees. The name occurs eight times in this Greek corpus, in Joshua, Judges, and 1 Maccabees. Because no verse text is provided, its particular historical significance cannot be explained here; the lexical meaning itself is simply the place-name Thamnatha.

This word is the proper name “Thekōe” or “Thekoe.” It functions as a name rather than a common term, so it identifies a particular biblical person, place, or other named entity rather than expressing an action or quality. It occurs six times in the Greek LXX corpus: five times in Old Testament books and once in 1 Maccabees. The name appears in passages from 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and 1 Maccabees.

This verb means to lament—to express grief or sorrow openly. It describes the act of mourning, whether for a person, a people, or a painful situation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 19 times, showing a recurring word for voiced grief rather than a rare or isolated expression. Its exact force in any verse depends on who is lamenting and what loss or trouble surrounds the word.

This word means “medical treatment”—care intended to address illness or injury. It is a noun, naming the treatment itself rather than the person who provides it or the condition being treated. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Exodus, 2 Chronicles, and Jeremiah. Its basic sense remains focused on physical care and recovery, while the surrounding passage determines the particular situation in which that treatment is mentioned.

Ieoul, also written Ieul, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs twice in the Greek Septuagint corpus, appearing once in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. Its occurrence in these genealogical passages shows that it functions as a person's name, while the available information does not provide a broader lexical meaning beyond the name itself.

“Priesthood” refers to the office, service, or standing connected with priests. It describes priestly responsibility as a recognized role rather than a single act of worship. In this Greek LXX corpus, the word occurs seven times, appearing once in 1 Chronicles and six times in later Jewish writings. Its central meaning remains the priestly office or ministry, while the surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis falls on the people who serve, their appointment, or their duties.

This verb means “appease”: to act so that displeasure is quieted or a person is satisfied. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs 11 times across 10 verses, from Exodus through Lamentations, showing that it is used in several Old Testament settings while retaining this central sense. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Kathoēl; Kathil is a proper name, functioning as a personal designation rather than a general description or action. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 14:7. The available meaning is limited to these name forms, so the word should be understood as identifying someone named Kathoēl or Kathil, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific identity and role involved. It is not presented as a common noun, verb, or abstract quality.

This word means tin, the metal. It is a noun naming a material rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times: four times in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its uses include descriptions of metals and objects made from them, so the word keeps its straightforward material meaning rather than expressing a figurative idea by itself. The surrounding verse determines how tin functions in each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “weigh down”: to burden something or someone so that movement or action becomes harder. It describes the effect of added weight, whether literally or in a comparable sense. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 14:26 and Joel 2:8. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains placing weight or a burden upon something.

This LXX word means “shut up” or “kept inside.” It describes someone or something enclosed, confined, or prevented from going out. As an adjective or noun, it can identify a person or thing in that restrained condition. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being confined and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “pacify”: to calm or bring a troubled situation under control. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense is therefore the act of quieting conflict, agitation, or unrest. The surrounding passage determines whether the calming concerns people, circumstances, or a broader disturbance, but the central idea remains bringing something unsettled toward peace.

This noun means “head” or “top.” It can refer to the head as a bodily part, or to the uppermost point of something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 373 times, so its ordinary meaning is broad but consistent: a physical head or the highest part. The word appears from Genesis through Song of Songs and is also used in descriptions involving people, animals, and objects. The precise force in any passage depends on what is being described.

This Greek LXX verb means “surge”: to rise or move with force, like something swelling forward in a powerful motion. It describes an active movement rather than a still condition. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at Isaiah 57:20. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its comparison, but the central idea remains forceful rising or turbulent movement.

This verb means “cry”: to cry out or express something aloud. It describes an outward vocal expression rather than a silent thought, and it may be used when a person calls to others or appeals for help. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears 60 times, showing that this is a recurring biblical way to describe crying. It occurs throughout the Old Testament portion of the LXX and in related Greek writings, including Psalms, Jeremiah, Isaiah, and Job. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “secretly” or “in secret.” It is an adverb describing an action done privately, hidden from others, or without public notice. In the Greek Old Testament and Greek Deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs three times, so its central sense remains focused and consistent rather than broad or varied. The surrounding passage determines exactly what action is being done secretly, but the word itself points to the concealed manner of that action.

This Greek LXX noun means “earthen pot,” referring to a container made from baked clay. It names an ordinary household vessel rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 1 Samuel 2:14. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a clay or earthen container.

This noun refers to loud, distressed crying—“shrieking” or “wailing.” It describes an audible expression of grief, pain, or anguish rather than a quiet feeling. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 6:32. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning is a loud, sorrowful cry.

This noun refers to daintiness or greediness—an undue concern for pleasurable food or self-indulgent appetite. It describes a disposition or tendency rather than an action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 6:36. The surrounding verse is needed to determine which aspect is emphasized there, but the word’s basic sense points to refined appetite or eager desire for more than is fitting.

Maazia is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Nehemiah 10:9, identifying an individual named in that passage. The name itself does not provide a broader definition or spiritual idea; its significance comes from the person and setting identified by the surrounding text. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the individual’s particular role cannot be explained from the name alone.

The word means “Madianitis,” a designation for someone identified with Madian. It functions as both a noun and an adjective, so it can name a person or describe something connected with Madian. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Numbers 25:6, 25:14, and 25:15. The precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains an identification with Madian.

e.h: A Word for Last A Long Time
e.t: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “last a long time”. It describes continuing over an extended period rather than ending quickly. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Deuteronomy, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though it is uncommon. The word is associated with Deuteronomy 17:20 and 32:27, but the precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its focus is duration: something continues or remains for a long time.

This adjective means “louder,” describing a sound or voice that has greater volume than another. It expresses comparison in intensity rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 8:12. The precise force of the comparison depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is an increase in loudness. This word should therefore be understood as describing how strongly something is heard, not automatically as expressing anger, importance, or authority.

This Greek LXX verb means “migrate”: to move from one place to another, especially as people relocate. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its sense is expressed by what someone does. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both in 2 Maccabees 2:1–2. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains movement away from one place to another.

This Greek LXX verb means “remove” or “cause to flee.” It describes taking something or someone away, or making them flee from a place or situation. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all in Psalms. Its basic sense remains focused on displacement: something is moved away, or a person is driven to flee. The precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea is removal or causing flight.

Nabdeēl, also rendered Navthil, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs three times in the LXX corpus: twice in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance as a person’s name comes from the surrounding genealogical or family context, which is not included here; the lexical meaning available is the name itself, not an additional description of the person.

Noumēnios, also rendered Numinios, is a proper name referring to a person rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, the name occurs four times, all in 1 Maccabees. The available references identify its repeated use, but without the surrounding verse text they do not establish additional meaning about the person’s role or character. Its meaning is therefore simply the personal name Noumēnios or Numinios.

This Greek LXX noun means “home” or “household.” It can refer to a dwelling place, the people belonging to that home, or the household as a family unit. The word is broadly used across the Greek Old Testament, occurring 1,490 times, so its precise sense in a verse depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes a place, family, or household group. It appears throughout the Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, including passages translated from Genesis through Song of Songs.

This word means “act of naming”: naming itself rather than the person or thing being named. It is a noun describing the act or practice of giving a name. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at Sirach 23:9. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the act of naming.

This word means “appearance” or “vision”—something seen, especially a displayed or revealed sight. It is a noun used for what comes into view or is perceived, and it can describe a vision associated with prophetic revelation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 102 times, with frequent use in Ezekiel and Daniel and additional appearances in books such as Genesis, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its central idea remains a visible appearance or vision, while the surrounding passage determines whether the word refers to ordinary appearance or a revealed sight.

This noun means “oath-swearing” or “being sworn in”—the act of binding someone through a solemn oath. It refers to the making or receiving of an oath rather than to a general promise or ordinary statement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel 17:18–19. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the solemn obligation created by an oath.

This Greek word means “tail,” referring to the rear or trailing part of an animal. It is a noun used for a physical body part, and its ordinary sense remains consistent across its eight occurrences in the Greek Old Testament. The word appears in passages from Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, Job, and Isaiah. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but the word itself denotes a tail rather than a broader symbolic idea.

This Greek LXX verb describes poising or swaying. It expresses the act of holding a poised position or moving with a swaying motion, depending on how it functions in its sentence. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Ezra, so its recorded use is limited to those two occurrences. Its basic idea remains physical balance or movement rather than a broad abstract concept.

This Greek LXX verb means to “take along” or “receive.” It describes bringing someone or something with you, or accepting what is given or entrusted. As an action word, it focuses on actively taking or welcoming rather than merely seeing or possessing. It occurs 33 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what or whom the subject takes or receives.

This Greek LXX noun refers to “goading” or a “paroxysm”—an intense, forceful agitation or outburst. It can describe pressure that provokes a response or a sudden surge of powerful feeling or action. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Deuteronomy and once in Jeremiah. Its exact emphasis—provoking pressure or an intense episode—depends on how it functions in the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX noun means “poor,” referring to a person who lacks material resources or lives in poverty. It is used broadly across the Greek Old Testament and related writings, appearing 75 times, including many occurrences in Psalms and Proverbs. The word describes poverty as a recognizable human condition, without by itself explaining its cause or the person’s character. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “rent round about” or “torn all over.” It describes something being ripped extensively, with the tearing reaching around or across it rather than being limited to one small place. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 10:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning centers on thorough or widespread tearing.

This adjective describes something that is “out of tune.” It points to a lack of harmony or proper agreement, like a sound that does not fit with the surrounding music. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 10:7. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, its exact force in that passage cannot be stated more specifically; its established meaning remains “out of tune.”

This noun refers to something made or produced—a “product”—or to a “poem.” It can therefore name a work that has been brought into existence, whether understood as a created product or a poetic composition. The word appears 29 times in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX, with most occurrences in Ecclesiastes. Its precise emphasis depends on how the surrounding sentence uses it, but its central idea remains something made or formed, including a poem as a kind of produced work.

This noun means “practicality”: the quality of dealing with something in a useful, workable way. It refers to the practical side of a matter rather than merely an idea or intention. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs seven times across six verses, including passages in 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Daniel, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains concern with practical activity or application.

This verb means “speak on the part of,” describing speech offered on behalf of another person or group. It presents or supports someone else’s case rather than focusing only on the speaker’s own position. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:48. The surrounding verse would be needed to determine exactly whom the speaker represented and what was being said there.

This verb means “pay attention” or “beware.” It calls a person to notice carefully and remain alert, especially when there may be danger, error, or something important that must not be ignored. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 117 times, so it expresses a recurring biblical call to attentive, watchful conduct rather than a single isolated action. Its precise force in any verse depends on what the surrounding passage says a person must notice or avoid.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “strike with the heel.” It describes the action of using the heel to hit or wound, and it functions as an action word rather than a name or description. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, in five verses from Genesis, Jeremiah, Hosea, and Malachi. Its central idea remains a physical act of striking with the heel, while the surrounding verse determines its particular force.

Rehoboam is a personal name referring to the son of Solomon and king of Judah. As a noun and proper name, it identifies one particular biblical person rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, the name occurs 62 times, most often in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles. Its meaning here is simply the person named Rehoboam; understanding what happens in any particular passage requires that passage’s surrounding text.

Seppham, also rendered Sepfam, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament wording, but the available lexical information does not provide a further underlying meaning. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Numbers 34:11. Its precise reference there must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage, since a name by itself mainly identifies rather than explains an action or quality.

Somnan is a proper name used to identify a named figure in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general term describing an action, quality, or object, but as a personal designation. This name occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Kings 19:2 and Isaiah 22:15 and 37:2. The available meaning is therefore the name itself: Somnan.

This word means “cushion,” referring to a soft support used for sitting, resting, or making a place more comfortable. It is a noun, so it names the object rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Ruth 3:7 and Isaiah 55:13. Its exact significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun means “computation”: the act of working something out by calculation or careful reckoning. It refers to a process of arriving at a result through thought or calculation, rather than to a person or object. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament tradition, once in Exodus and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains calculation or mental reckoning.

This Greek LXX verb means to linger together—to remain with someone rather than leave immediately. It describes staying alongside another person, with the emphasis on continued presence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 71:5. Because the verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage must be understood from its surrounding context. Its basic sense remains clear: two or more people continue together for a time.

This verb means to flee along with someone else—to escape together rather than flee alone. It describes joined movement away from danger or pursuit, with the idea of accompanying others in their flight. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 1 and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one passage depends on who is fleeing and what threat or circumstance prompts the escape, but the central meaning remains shared flight or retreat with others.

This verb means “play the,” describing the act of producing music with something identified by the surrounding sentence. Its precise object is not included in the word’s basic meaning, so the verse context determines what is being played. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 13 times, showing a repeated musical action rather than a person, place, or abstract idea.

This adverb means “completely,” describing something done or existing in a full and entire way. It adds emphasis to the action or condition it modifies, indicating that nothing essential is lacking or left unfinished. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, all in deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains completeness or wholeness. This Greek LXX verb means “cheer”: to bring gladness or give joy. It describes an action that lifts or delights someone rather than merely naming a feeling. The word appears ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, including passages in Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the giving or experiencing of joy.

This verb means to wound—to injure someone or cause bodily harm. It describes the act of striking or damaging a person, rather than merely referring to a wound as a condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 18 times, so its basic sense is consistently connected with physical injury. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This adjective describes something as “hyacinth blue,” identifying its color. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for blue-colored materials and objects, including parts of the tabernacle furnishings and priestly clothing. The word occurs 26 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, especially in Numbers and Exodus. Its basic function is descriptive: it marks a visible blue color rather than expressing an action, emotion, or abstract quality.

This noun means “high water mark,” referring to the level reached by water. It occurs once in the Greek Septuagint, at Ezekiel 47:11. The word therefore names a measurable boundary or limit associated with water, rather than describing water generally. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the sentence uses this boundary term.

Pharathōn is a proper name rendered as “Pharathōn” or “Farathon.” It identifies a particular place or designation rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs twice: once in 1 Chronicles and once in 1 Maccabees. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish further details about the place or its significance. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the name Pharathōn, also written Farathon in English.

Phetaia, also rendered Fetea, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 24:16. Because the available meaning is the name itself and no verse text is provided here, its ordinary significance is simply identification of a person named Phetaia or Fetea. The surrounding passage would be needed to explain that person’s specific role or importance in the verse.

This adjective means “widowed”: it describes a person whose spouse has died. As a describing word, it identifies someone in that condition rather than naming an action, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 54:4, so this is a rare word in that corpus. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains “widowed.”

This word is a proper name, rendered “Chountha” or “Khuntha.” It identifies a person or place by name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 17:24. Without the surrounding verse text, the specific person or place identified there cannot be described further, but the word’s basic function is clear: it is a name used as a distinctive designation.

This word means “shoulder,” referring to the part of the body between the neck and upper arm. As a noun, it can describe a person’s shoulder or shoulders, and it may also identify the shoulder area of something carried or worn. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 50 times, including descriptions involving clothing and carrying burdens. Its use in passages such as Exodus 28:12 and Joshua 4:5 reflects the ordinary physical sense of the shoulder as a place for bearing or supporting something.

This word is a personal name, referring to Hōsēe, also written Osie. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 14 times across 13 verses, including passages in 1 Samuel, 2 Kings, Nehemiah, and Hosea. Its exact reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function remains the same: naming the person called Hōsēe or Osie.
